chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Policy Flows Into Asset Prices

lessons.title: Equities and Rates: Valuations, Rate-Sensitive Sectors, and the Nifty

body.text: A share is a claim on profits that arrive over many years, and every future rupee of profit is worth less today when interest rates are higher. That single idea explains why the Nifty often falls when the RBI turns hawkish, why real estate and bank stocks react first, and why a rate cut can lift some sectors while doing almost nothing for others.

children.text: In the last lesson you saw that bond yields move first. Stocks follow, but not all in the same way. This lesson explains the two channels through which interest rates reach equity prices, which sectors feel them most, and how to read the relationship between the Nifty and the 10-year G-Sec yield.
Channel 1: The Discount Rate

markDefs.definition: The annual return investors require to hold an investment, used to convert future cash flows into today's value. It is built from the risk-free rate, usually the G-Sec yield, plus a premium for risk.

children.text: The value of any business is the present value of all the cash it will generate in the future. To convert future cash into today's rupees, investors use a
discount rate
: roughly the risk-free G-Sec yield plus a premium for the extra risk of owning shares. When G-Sec yields rise, the discount rate rises, and the same future profits are worth less today.

body.latex: \text{Value today} = \dfrac{\text{Cash flow next year}}{\text{Discount rate} - \text{Growth rate}}
body.caption: The simple growing perpetuity model, a stripped-down version of a discounted cash flow valuation

children.text: Take a company that will generate ₹100 of cash next year, growing 8% a year forever. If investors require 12%, it is worth ₹100 ÷ (0.12 − 0.08) = ₹2,500.

body.title: What Does Half a Percent Do?
body.prompt: Bond yields rise and investors now require 12.5% instead of 12% from the same company: ₹100 of cash next year, growing at 8% forever. By what percentage does its value change? Enter a negative number for a fall, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: New value = ₹100 ÷ (0.125 − 0.08) = ₹2,222. Change = (₹2,222 − ₹2,500) ÷ ₹2,500 × 100 = -11.1%. A half-point rise in the required return wiped out about a ninth of the company's value, without a single change to its business.

body.text: The effect is strongest for companies whose profits lie far in the future. A fast-growing company valued at 80 times earnings depends on cash flows decades away, so rising rates hurt it much more than a mature company paying steady dividends today. Investors call these "long duration" stocks, borrowing the idea from bonds.

children.text: Channel 2: Earnings

Rates also change the profits themselves. Companies with heavy borrowings pay more interest when rates rise. Customers who buy on EMIs, such as homes, cars and two-wheelers, buy less when loans get dearer. And banks see their margins, credit growth and bond portfolios all shift at once.

markDefs.definition: Sectors whose earnings or valuations depend heavily on interest rates, such as banks, NBFCs, real estate and autos. They tend to rally on rate cuts and fall on rate hike fears.

children.text: Stocks in the first five rows are called
rate-sensitive sectors
. FMCG, IT and pharma are often called defensives, because their earnings depend far less on the cost of credit.
The Bank Margin Twist

markDefs.definition: The difference between the interest a bank earns on loans and investments and the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings, as a percentage of its earning assets.

children.text: You might expect banks to love rate cuts. It is more complicated. Most retail and MSME loans are now linked to the repo rate and reset within three months, but fixed deposits reprice only as they mature. So when the RBI cuts, loan yields fall quickly while deposit costs fall slowly, squeezing the
net interest margin (NIM)
for a few quarters. Cuts help banks through faster loan growth and gains on their bond portfolios, not through wider margins.

body.title: Which Stock Is Most Rate-Sensitive?
body.question: The market suddenly starts pricing in an RBI rate hike. Which of these is likely to be hit hardest, all else equal?
options: An FMCG company with no debt selling soaps and biscuits
An IT services company earning mostly in US dollars
A real estate developer with high debt selling homes mostly bought on home loans
A pharma company exporting generic drugs
body.explanation: The developer is hit through both channels: higher rates raise its own borrowing costs and make home loan EMIs more expensive for its buyers. The FMCG company has no debt and little loan-driven demand. The IT and pharma exporters may even benefit if higher uncertainty weakens the rupee, since they earn in foreign currency.

children.text: Case 1: A Cut That Lifted the Rate-Sensitives, 6 June 2025

When the RBI surprised with a 50 basis point cut and a 100 basis point CRR cut, the stock market rallied, and the rate-sensitive sectors led. The Nifty 50 rose 1.02% to close at 25,003.05. The Nifty Realty index jumped nearly 5%, the Nifty Auto index gained over 1%, and the Nifty Bank index hit a record high of 56,695 during the day.

body.text: Notice the contrast with the bond market from Lesson 4 of Chapter 2. On the same day, the 10-year yield closed higher because of the RBI's neutral stance and "very limited space" comment. Equity investors cheered the size of the cut; bond traders focused on the signal that cuts were ending. Different markets can read the same policy differently.

children.text: Case 2: Rate Hike Fears Return, September 2026

Fifteen months later, the mood had reversed. CPI inflation was projected to peak at 5.9%, the August MPC minutes had put rate hikes on the table, Brent crude was near $97, and the 10-year G-Sec yield was pushing towards 7%. Across the world, US Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had said at Jackson Hole in late August that the Fed still had "work to do" on inflation, and futures markets priced a high chance of a September Fed hike.

On 11 September 2026, as the RBI announced OMO bond sales and yields rose, rate-sensitive stocks sold off. The Nifty Realty index fell as much as 4.5% during the day, with Lodha down about 7%, before closing 2.70% lower at 848.5, down 5% over the month. Bank and auto stocks also came under pressure. The Nifty 50 closed at 23,398.10, down 0.34%.

body.title: How Far Has the Nifty Moved?
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 closed at 25,003.05 on 6 June 2025 and at 23,398.10 on 11 September 2026. What is the percentage change? Enter a negative number for a fall, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (23,398.10 − 25,003.05) ÷ 25,003.05 × 100 = -6.42%. Over the same period the 10-year G-Sec yield rose from 6.29% to about 6.96%. Rates are not the only thing that moved stocks in those fifteen months, but rising yields made Indian equities less attractive relative to safe bonds.

children.text: Case 3: The 2022 Global Tightening

The biggest recent test came in 2022, when the US Fed and the RBI hiked aggressively. The Nifty 50 fell from its peak of 18,604 in October 2021 to a low near 15,183 in June 2022. Foreign portfolio investors sold a record net ₹1.21 lakh crore of Indian shares in 2022, more than double the previous record set in 2008, as higher US rates pulled global money back home.

body.text: Higher interest rates abroad matter as much as at home. When US Treasury yields rise, global investors can earn more in dollars with less risk, so they pull money out of emerging markets like India. That is why a Fed Chair's speech at Jackson Hole can move the Nifty.

children.text: The Earnings Yield vs Bond Yield Test

markDefs.definition: A company's or index's earnings divided by its price, the inverse of the PE ratio. It shows how much profit each ₹100 invested in the stock or index earns.

children.text: A simple way to compare stocks and bonds is the
earnings yield

: flip the PE ratio upside down. If the Nifty trades at a PE of 20, every ₹100 invested buys ₹5 of annual earnings, an earnings yield of 5%. Compare that with the 10-year G-Sec yield, which you can earn with virtually no default risk.

body.caption: Compare with the 10-year G-Sec yield to judge relative value

body.title: Stocks vs Bonds in September 2026
body.prompt: On 11 September 2026, the Nifty 50 PE ratio was about 19.78 and the 10-year G-Sec yield was about 6.96%. What is the Nifty's earnings yield, in percent, rounded to two decimal places?
body.explanation: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ 19.78 × 100 = 5.06%. The G-Sec yield of 6.96% is 1.90 percentage points higher. That does not mean bonds are simply better: company earnings grow over time, while a bond's coupon is fixed. But the wider this gap, the more growth equity investors are relying on to justify owning shares instead of safe bonds.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why the Bond-Equity Comparison Is Only a Rough Guide

children.text: Comparing an earnings yield with a bond yield, sometimes called the Fed model, is appealing but imperfect.
Earnings grow over time; a bond's coupon never does. A 5% earnings yield growing at 12% a year can beat a 7% bond comfortably over a decade.
The Nifty's PE is based on reported earnings, which swing with the economic cycle. A low PE at the top of an earnings boom can be misleading.
Inflation affects both. High inflation pushes bond yields up, but companies with pricing power can pass costs on and grow earnings in rupee terms.

Use the comparison to understand direction: when bond yields rise sharply while earnings forecasts stay flat, equity valuations usually come under pressure. Do not use it as a precise buy or sell signal.

body.title: Is Your Portfolio Positioned for Rate Hikes?
body.scenario: Your friend's ₹10 lakh equity portfolio holds 30% in real estate developers, 25% in NBFCs, 20% in private banks, 15% in auto stocks and 10% in an IT services company. It is September 2026: the RBI is hinting at possible hikes, the 10-year G-Sec yield is near 7%, and the US Fed is also leaning hawkish.
body.prompt: How exposed is this portfolio to rising rates, and what questions should your friend ask before making any changes?
body.modelAnswer: The portfolio is heavily exposed: about 90% sits in sectors that are directly hurt by higher rates, through higher borrowing costs, weaker loan-driven demand or pressure on valuations. Only the 10% in IT is relatively insulated, and IT may even gain if the rupee weakens. Before acting, your friend should ask: Why do I own these stocks? If it is for long-term business quality, a temporary rate cycle may not change the thesis. How much debt do the specific companies carry? A cash-rich developer is very different from a heavily leveraged one. Are hikes already priced in? Realty had already fallen 5% in a month by 11 September. And does the portfolio match my risk tolerance? Rather than trading on rate forecasts, a more durable fix is diversification, adding defensives like FMCG and pharma, or some fixed income, so that no single interest rate scenario can do this much damage.

points: Rates reach stocks through two channels: the discount rate applied to future profits, and the direct effect on company earnings.
Higher G-Sec yields raise the discount rate, hitting high-growth, high-PE stocks hardest because their profits lie furthest in the future.
Real estate, banks, NBFCs, autos and infrastructure are rate-sensitive; FMCG, IT and pharma are relatively defensive.
Rate cuts help banks mainly through loan growth and bond gains, while margins can shrink for a few quarters as loans reprice faster than deposits.
The June 2025 cut lifted Nifty Realty nearly 5%; the September 2026 hike fears sent it down 2.70% in a day and 5% in a month.
The Nifty's earnings yield of about 5.06% against a G-Sec yield near 6.96% shows how rising bond yields raise the bar for equities.
